I am using three datasets to explore my research questions about spending and crime rates in Washington state counties.

### 1. How many offenses were logged in each county in 2025?

```{python}
#dependencies
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pyprojroot import here

#importing crime dataset
file_path = here('projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/wa_crime_2025.csv')
crime_2025 = pd.read_csv(file_path)
```

'crime_2025' is a dataset containing observations of all offenses logged by every police department in Washington in 2025. Each offense also notes the county corresponding to the department that logged it. I want to sum the number of offenses by county.

```{python}
crime_2025.columns.tolist()
```

```{python}
#cleaning 

#dropping columns I'm not interested in
crime_2025_clean = crime_2025.drop(columns=["Reference Number", "Victim", "ORI", "Location", "Agency"])

#remove caps lock
crime_2025_clean["County"] = crime_2025_clean["County"].str.title()

#let's get total counts of the number of the offenses in each county in 2025
county_crime_2025 = (crime_2025_clean
    .groupby("County")
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="Total Offenses"))

#there's a county listed in crime called "state agency" I am dropping before joining
county_crime_2025 = county_crime_2025[county_crime_2025["County"] != "State Agency"]

#county_crime_2025 
```

I choose to drop a column called State Agency, which listed 620 offenses in 2025. After some brief research, I have not been able to determine what State Agency means in this context, but I suspect those may be offenses logged by the Washington State Patrol. Since I am looking at counties specifically, and I do not have spending data for "State Agency", I choose to drop this column.

### 2. How many offenses were violent and how many were nonviolent? 

Now I'm going to use the 'crime_2025_clean' data that lists all offenses to sum by violent and nonviolent crime.

```{python}
#let's see all of the offenses
crime_2025_clean["Offense"].unique()

#now I'll divide based on FBI UCR definitions of violent & other crime
violent_offenses = [
    "Murder Non Negligent Manslaughter",
    "Rape",
    "Robbery",
    "Aggravated Assault"]

#sorting into violent and other
crime_2025_clean["Crime Type"] = np.where(
    crime_2025_clean["Offense"].isin(violent_offenses),
    "Violent",
    "Other")

#sum types of crime by county
county_crime_type = (crime_2025_clean
    .groupby(["County", "Crime Type"])
    .size()
    .unstack(fill_value=0)
    .reset_index())

#see violent, other, and total all in one df
county_crime_type["Total Offenses"] = (
    county_crime_type["Violent"] +
    county_crime_type["Other"])

#drop 'State Agency' in this df too
county_crime_type = county_crime_type[county_crime_type["County"] != "State Agency"]

#county_crime_type
```

Deciding how to define "violent crime" in this case was difficult because the offenses listed in this dataset are not specific. I initially wanted to use Washington state law's definition of a violent offense, but it defines violent crime by degree. For example, rape in the first degree is classified as a violent offense but rape in the second degree is not ([Source](https://app.leg.wa.gov/rcw/default.aspx?cite=9.94A.030)). My data simply lists 'Rape', so I don't feel that I have the ability use the Washington state legal definition without proper specification. I insteaed defined violent crime using the common crime statistics defintion, which is based on the FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting defintion. UCR lists the following as violent offenses (no matter the degree): murder and nonnegligent manslaughter, rape, robbery, and aggravated assault. I choose to label the categories "Violent" and "Other" because crimes that don't fall into the FBI's definition of violent crime are not necessarily nonviolent.

### 3. How much do Washington state counties spend on law enforcement activities? How much do counties spend on social services?

```{python}
file_lawenf = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/fit_lawenforcementactivities.csv")
fit_lawenforcement = pd.read_csv(file_lawenf, skiprows=6)

file_social = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/fit_socialservices.csv")
fit_social = pd.read_csv(file_social, skiprows=6)
```

```{python}
#sort into counties
fit_le_counties = fit_lawenforcement[fit_lawenforcement["Governments/$ Dollars"].str.endswith("County", na=False)]

#39 counties total in WA
#len(fit_le_counties) #output is 39!

#social services data
fit_social_counties = fit_social[fit_social["Governments/$ Dollars"].str.endswith("County", na=False)]

#39 counties total in WA
#len(fit_social_counties) #output is 39!
```

```{python}
#cleaning dollar values in the data
fit_le_counties["2025"] = (fit_le_counties["2025"]
    .str.replace("$", "", regex=False)
    .str.replace(",", "", regex=False))
fit_le_counties["2025"] = pd.to_numeric(fit_le_counties["2025"], errors="coerce" ) #some unexpected values in the dollar column, so replacing these with NaN

#cleaning dollar values in the data
fit_social_counties["2025"] = (fit_social_counties["2025"]
    .str.replace("$", "", regex=False)
    .str.replace(",", "", regex=False))
fit_social_counties["2025"] = pd.to_numeric(fit_social_counties["2025"], errors="coerce" ) #some unexpected values in the dollar column, so replacing these with NaN
```

In the law enforcement spending dataset, law enforcement activities include police operations, traffic policing, administration, crime prevention, training, facilities, and property and evidence room. In the social spending dataset, social services include homeless services, mental health services, public safety services, chemical dependency services, welfare, child services, aging and disability services, veterans services, developmental disability services, and domestic violence services.

### 4. Do counties spend more on law enforcement activities or social services, on average?

```{python}
#dropping the columns that I don't want to be present in the eventual joined df
fit_le_counties = fit_le_counties[["Governments/$ Dollars", "2025"]]

fit_social_counties = fit_social_counties[["Governments/$ Dollars", "2025"]]

#these dataframes had a different name for the 'County' column
fit_le_counties = fit_le_counties.rename(columns={
    "Governments/$ Dollars": "County",
    "2025": "Law Enforcement Spending"})

fit_social_counties = fit_social_counties.rename(columns={
    "Governments/$ Dollars": "County",
    "2025": "Social Spending"})

fit_le_counties["County"] = fit_le_counties["County"].str.replace(" County", "", regex=False)

fit_social_counties["County"] = fit_social_counties["County"].str.replace(" County", "", regex=False)

spending = fit_le_counties.merge(fit_social_counties,on="County")

#spending[["Law Enforcement Spending", "Social Spending"]].mean()
```

In 2025, Washington counties spent an average of $24,960,060 on law enforcement and $65,967,350 on social services.

Now I am joining together the spending data, crime data, and population data.

```{python}
#population data
file_pop = here("projects/wa-state-police-social-spending/_data/populations.csv")
population = pd.read_csv(file_pop)

#only want county name
population["County"] = population["County"].str.removeprefix(".")
population["County"] = population["County"].str.replace(" County, Washington", "", regex=False)

#just 2025
population = population[["County", "2025"]]
#rename year for clarity in joined df
population = population.rename(columns={"2025": "2025 Population"})

#removing comma and converting from string
population["2025 Population"] = (population["2025 Population"].str.replace(",", "", regex=False))
population["2025 Population"] = pd.to_numeric(population["2025 Population"], errors="coerce" )

#population
```

```{python}
#joining crime, spending, and population dfs
county_data_2025 = (fit_le_counties
    .merge(fit_social_counties, on="County", how="outer")
    .merge(county_crime_type, on="County", how="outer")
    .merge(population, on="County", how="outer"))

#county_data_2025
#county_data_2025[county_data_2025.isna().any(axis=1)]
```

Benton, Chelan, Grant, and Thurston Counties do not have spending data. This is consistent with the data source which explains that "These governments historically report in this dollar category, but have not filed or are currently editing their FY 2025 filing". These counties will be excluded from analysis for now but hopefully can be included later. 

### 5. Do counties with higher police spending have more offenses?

```{python}
#dropping the 4 counties with missing spending data
plot = county_data_2025[["Law Enforcement Spending", "Total Offenses"]].dropna()

#making a scatterplot to represent law enforcement spending and total offenses
x = plot["Law Enforcement Spending"]
y = plot["Total Offenses"]
plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Law Enforcement Spending")
plt.ylabel("Total Offenses")
plt.title("Law Enforcement Spending and Total Offenses by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()
```

This scatterplot shows a strong positive relationship between law enforcement spending and total offenses by county. This relationship can be explained by population differences.

### 6. What's the crime rate in each Washington state county?

```{python}
#calculating crime rate (crime rate = numnber of crimes per 100k people)
county_data_2025["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"] = (county_data_2025["Total Offenses"] / county_data_2025["2025 Population"]) * 100000

#county_data_2025

#county_data_2025[["County", "Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]].sort_values("Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)", ascending=False)
```

Spokane, Garfield, and Benton counties have the highest crime rates. Crime rate captures the number of offenses per 100,000 people, calculated using population and number of total offenses.

### 7. Do counties with higher crime rates have more law enforcement spending?

```{python}
#per capita spending
county_data_2025["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"] = (county_data_2025["Law Enforcement Spending"] / county_data_2025["2025 Population"])

county_data_2025["Social Spending Per Capita"] = (county_data_2025["Social Spending"] / county_data_2025["2025 Population"])

#county_data_2025
```

```{python}
#scatterplot
plot2 = county_data_2025[["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)", "Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"]].dropna()

x = plot2["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]
y = plot2["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Offenses per 100,000 People")
plt.ylabel("Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita")
plt.title("Crime Rate and Law Enforcement Spending by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()
```

There is a weak relationship between crime rates and law enforcement spending per capita. The line of best fit is very slightly negatively sloped. Counties are widely dispersed around the line of best fit, which suggests that counties with higher crime rates do not always spend more per capita on law enforcement. Some counties stand out on this plot as they have high per capita law enforcement spending relative to the rest of the state's counties.

```{python}
#correlation coefficient
plot2["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"].corr(plot2["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"])
```

The correlation coefficient between crime rate and law enforcement spending per capita is -0.037, meaning there's essentially no linear relationship between these variables.

### Do counties with higher crime rates have more social spending?

```{python}
#scatterplot
plot3 = county_data_2025[["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)", "Social Spending Per Capita"]].dropna()

x = plot3["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]
y = plot3["Social Spending Per Capita"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Offenses per 100,000 People")
plt.ylabel("Social Spending Per Capita")
plt.title("Crime Rate and Social Spending by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()
```

There is a negative relationship between crime rates and social spending per capita. The line of best fit is negatively sloped. Counties with higher crime rates appear to generally spend less per capita on social services. There is a lot of variation among counties which suggests that crime rates alone do not explain differences in social spending.

```{python}
#correlation coefficient
plot3["Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"].corr(plot3["Social Spending Per Capita"])
```

The correlation coefficient between crime rate and law enforcement spending per capita is -0.226, meaning there's a weak negative realtionship between the variables.

### 8. Do counties with higher law enforcement spending have lower violent crime rates?

```{python}
#calculating violent crime rate
county_data_2025["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"] = (county_data_2025["Violent"] / county_data_2025["2025 Population"]) * 100000
```

```{python}
plot4 = county_data_2025[["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita", "Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]].dropna()

x = plot4["Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita"]
y = plot4["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Law Enforcement Spending Per Capita")
plt.ylabel("Violent Offenses per 100,000 People")
plt.title("Law Enforcement Spending and Violent Crime Rate by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()
```

There is a positive relationship between law enforcement spending per capita and violent crime rates, which challenged my assumption that greater spending would be associated with lower violent crime. There is an extreme outlier in the upper right corner of the plot, which appears to be influencing the relationship. 

```{python}
#identify the outlier
county_data_2025.loc[county_data_2025["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"].idxmax()]
```

The outlier is Garfield County, which happens to be the smallest county (by population) in Washington state. This exposes a limitation in my calculation of crime rate - a county with a small population will get a high crime rate even with very few offenses.

### Do counties with higher social spending have lower violent crime rates?

```{python}
plot5 = county_data_2025[["Social Spending Per Capita", "Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]].dropna()

x = plot5["Social Spending Per Capita"]
y = plot5["Violent Offenses Per 100k (crime rate)"]

plt.scatter(x, y)

#line of best fit
m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
plt.plot(x, m*x + b)

plt.xlabel("Social Spending Per Capita")
plt.ylabel("Violent Offenses per 100,000 People")
plt.title("Social Spending and Violent Crime Rate by Washington State County (2025)")
plt.show()
```

This plot shows a slightly negative relationship between social spending per capita and violent crime rates, meaning higher social spending per capita is associated with a lower violent crime rate. Once again, Garfield County is a major outlier.
